Title: DGLight: DQN-Guided GRPO Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models for Traffic Signal Control
Text:
DGLight: DQN-Guided GRPO Fine-Tuning of Large Language
Models for Traffic Signal Control
Chenbo Yu
National University of Singapore
Singapore
yu.chenbo@u.nus.edu
Abstract
Traffic signal control (TSC) plays a central role in reducing con-
gestion and maintaining urban mobility. This dissertation intro-
duces DGLight, a critic-guided reinforcement-learning framework
for adapting a pretrained large language model to TSC. DGLight
first trains a CoLight-based Deep Q-Network critic to estimate
traffic-aware action values from structured intersection states, then
uses the frozen critic to score candidate language-model actions
and optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO). The resulting controller maps traffic states to interpretable
reasoning traces and signal decisions while learning from dense
per-state supervision rather than raw cumulative environment
rewards. Experiments on TSC benchmarks covering Jinan and
Hangzhou show that DGLight is the strongest overall method
among the compared LLM-based controllers, remains competi-
tive with strong RL baselines, and transfers well to city datasets
not used to fit the critic. Qualitative examples further show that
the model’s generated reasoning is interpretable and aligned with
the chosen signal phase. The project code is available at https:
//github.com/yyccbb/FYP_LLMTSC.

Introduction
Rapid urbanization and accelerating motorization have placed un-
precedented strain on urban transportation systems worldwide. As
cities densify, limited road infrastructure must accommodate ever-
growing travel demand, leading to persistent congestion, unreliable
travel times, and increased environmental externalities. Inefficient
traffic flow not only wastes fuel and economic productivity but also
amplifies air pollution and degrades quality of life, particularly in
densely populated urban corridors.
Traffic signal control (TSC) aims to coordinate phase sequences and
durations at signalized intersections to maximize throughput and
reduce congestion. Classical fixed-time methods use the Webster
formula (Yin, Dridi, and Moudni, 2015) to preset signal timings
based on historical traffic data collected from the traffic network at
different times. In contrast, the max-pressure control framework
(Mercader, Uwayid, and Haddad, 2020) computes a pressure value
for each signal phase from the difference between queue lengths on
opposing approaches and selects the phase with the highest pres-
sure; this strategy can be shown to maximize network throughput.
Reinforcement-learning (RL) methods model TSC as a Markov de-
cision process in which an agent observes traffic states (for ex-
ample, lane queue lengths and delays), chooses an action (phase
switch) and receives a reward linked to throughput or delay re-
duction. Deep RL further parameterizes the control policy using
neural networks, enabling the agent to approximate complex, high-
dimensional decision functions. Such methods have demonstrated
strong empirical performance across a wide range of simulated
traffic scenarios. However, they also introduce notable challenges.
In particular, learned policies often exhibit limited generalization,
as models trained in one traffic environment exhibit degraded per-
formance when deployed in different cities or under unseen con-
ditions. Furthermore, the reliance on opaque neural representa-
tions reduces interpretability, making it difficult to explain or verify
decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses a bar-
rier to real-world adoption, where reliability and accountability are
critical.
Large Language Models (LLMs) represent a new paradigm in ar-
tificial intelligence, combining strong reasoning ability with the
capacity to generate interpretable, text-based outputs. These prop-
erties make LLMs promising candidates for traffic signal control,
where decision transparency and adaptability are highly desirable.
By framing control as a reasoning process, LLM-based agents can
potentially provide both actionable policies and interpretable expla-
nations, bridging the gap between performance and interpretabil-
ity. However, this potential is not yet fully realized in practice.
Achieving real-time responsiveness typically requires deploying
smaller-scale models or mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures
with compact expert networks. Without sufficient domain adapta-
tion, such models often fail to capture complex traffic dynamics,
leading to suboptimal decisions.
To this end, I introduce DGLight, a critic-guided reinforcement-
learning framework for adapting a pretrained large language model
to traffic signal control. The framework combines a Deep Q-Network
(DQN) critic with GRPO-based policy optimization so that textual
traffic prompts can be scored using dense, traffic-aware action val-
ues. In this way, DGLight trains the language model to produce both

an interpretable reasoning trace and a valid signal decision, trans-
ferring value-based traffic knowledge into the policy to improve
decision quality across traffic settings.
The main contributions of this dissertation are:
• First, I propose the DGLight framework, which unifies a
value-based traffic critic and LLM fine-tuning within a sin-
gle critic-guided training pipeline.
• Second, I trained a TSC controller with DGLight by adapt-
ing a Llama3-8b traffic-signal model through the proposed
pipeline, yielding an interpretable language-based policy
for multi-intersection control.
• Third, I conduct comprehensive experiments on standard
TSC benchmarks, including baseline comparisons, transfer
evaluation on unseen city datasets, interpretability analysis,
and ablation studies, to validate the effectiveness of the
proposed method.
2
Related Work
Traffic Signal Control. Early TSC methods such as FixedTime (Yin
et al., 2015) rely on predefined cycle lengths and manually designed
phase splits for each intersection. Although these approaches are
simple and stable in practice, they adapt poorly to time-varying traf-
fic demand. MaxPressure (Mercader et al., 2020) improves adaptabil-
ity by selecting phases according to the queue imbalance between
incoming and outgoing directions, making it more responsive than
fixed plans. However, both FixedTime and MaxPressure remain con-
strained by handcrafted rules or preset logic, which limits their
flexibility under complex and highly dynamic traffic scenarios.
Recent progress in reinforcement learning has led to a series of RL-
based TSC methods. CoLight (Wei et al., 2019) models network-level
cooperation among intersections through graph attention, enabling
each signal to coordinate with surrounding intersections instead of
acting independently. CoSLight (Ruan et al., 2024) further extends
this idea by jointly optimizing signal control and collaborator se-
lection, so that each intersection can dynamically decide which
neighboring intersections are most useful for coordination under
current traffic conditions. MPLight (C. Chen et al., 2020) is a decen-
tralized and pressure-aware RL approach designed for large-scale
road networks, using parameter sharing to improve scalability and
training efficiency. Although these methods achieve strong perfor-
mance in per city simulation, RL-based controllers face challenges
in generalization and interpretability, hence deployment robustness
in real-world environments.
To address these limitations, recent studies have begun exploring
the integration of large language models (LLMs) into TSC. LLM-
Assisted Light (M. Wang et al., 2024) places an LLM at the center of
control and augments it with perception and decision-support tools
so that it can combine live traffic observations with established
TSC methods and remain robust under emergency, roadblock, and
sensor-outage scenarios. iLLM-TSC (Pang, M. Wang, Pun, C. S. Chen,
and X. Xiong, 2024) instead adopts a hybrid design in which an RL
controller first proposes an action and an LLM then verifies or ad-
justs that action when observations are degraded or rare events such
as packet loss and emergency vehicles fall outside the original RL
formulation. LATS (Y. Zhang, P. Li, Zhou, Fan, and Sartoretti, 2026)
further explores a teacher-student setting in which an LLM teacher
provides rich semantic features during multi-agent RL training,
while a smaller student controller learns to emulate those features
and is deployed without the LLM at inference time. LLMLight (Lai, Z.
Xu, W. Zhang, Liu, and H. Xiong, 2024) moves closer to end-to-end
LLM control by adapting its LightGPT backbone through imitation
fine-tuning and critic-guided policy refinement so that the model
can make direct signal decisions with improved interpretability and
cross-scenario performance. Traffic-R1 (Zou et al., 2025) extends
this trend with a 3B RL-finetuned foundation model that combines
expert-aligned offline training, online self-exploration, and asyn-
chronous multi-agent communication to achieve strong zero-shot
and out-of-distribution TSC performance. Compared with end-to-
end LLM finetuning, LLM+RL hybrids may remain inferior because
they still inherit the ceiling and failure modes of the underlying RL
controller. Existing end-to-end finetuning methods also have no-
table limitations: In LLMLight, the critic-guided policy refinement
objective is weaker than modern policy-gradient methods because
the reward/advantage magnitude does not directly participate in
loss computation. Traffic-R1, meanwhile, relies on substantial hu-
man effort to label the offline finetuning data, and its fixed-horizon
cumulative queue-based reward assigns the same coarse mean re-
ward to all steps within the horizon.
RL finetuning of LLMs. RL-based preference alignment (Ouyang
et al., 2022) adapts a pretrained LLM using scalar or pairwise feed-
back so that the policy is optimized toward preferred responses
rather than merely imitating target outputs. Among modern policy
optimization methods, TRPO (Schulman, Levine, Moritz, Jordan,
and Abbeel, 2015) constrains updates within a trust region to sta-
bilize improvement, PPO (Schulman, Wolski, Dhariwal, Radford,
and Klimov, 2017) replaces this with a clipped surrogate objective
that is simpler and more practical at scale, and GRPO (Shao et
al., 2024) further removes the separate value model by computing
group-relative advantages over sampled responses, which makes
it especially attractive for LLM training. Closely related to these
RL-style methods, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) performs direct pref-
erence optimization on chosen–rejected response pairs and avoids
explicit reward-model fitting and online rollout collection. This
line of work is particularly important because preference-aligned
RL can train reasoning ability rather than only answer imitation:
through exploration, comparison, and preference-based updates,
the model learns to assign higher probability to response trajec-
tories that exhibit stronger multi-step reasoning while remaining
close to a reference policy through KL regularization, as empha-
sized in RLHF-style alignment and recent reasoning-oriented RL
studies (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025).
Recent systems such as DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) show that
large-scale self-exploration can substantially improve reasoning
behavior, making RL preference alignment increasingly relevant for
domain-specific agents that must optimize long-horizon objectives.

rected graph consisting of intersections V and lanes L. The lane set

observing the number of vehicles in each segment of the lanes

4
Methodology
This section introduces DGLight, a two-stage reinforcement-learning
pipeline for adapting a pretrained large language model to traffic
signal control. In the first stage, a CoLight-based DQN critic is
trained to estimate action values for signal-phase decisions when
provided with structured environment states. In the second stage,
the frozen critic scores candidate LLM responses during rollout and
the scores are used as the reward signal for GRPO-based policy
optimization. Refer to Figure 1 for the pipeline architecture.
4.1
Pretraining the CoLight-Based DQN Critic
The critic used in DGLight is based on CoLight (Wei et al., 2019),
a graph-attentive deep Q-learning model for network-level traffic
signal control. CoLight is employed as a pretrained value estima-
tor so that the subsequent GRPO stage can query a traffic-aware
action-value function rather than rely exclusively on the raw en-
vironment reward. Given the current environment state, the critic
predicts action values for each intersection and thereby provides a
dense estimate of the quality of candidate signal phases under the
prevailing traffic situation.
The CoLight critic is composed of three main components. The
first component is an observation embedding module that trans-
forms the local traffic state of each intersection into a latent feature
representation. The second component consists of one or more
multi-head graph-attention layers, which propagate information
across neighboring intersections and produce attention-weighted
network representations. The final component is a Q-value predic-
tion layer that maps the aggregated features to one scalar value for
each admissible signal phase. This architecture combines local state
encoding, inter-intersection coordination, and value-based action
estimation within a single model.
Training follows the standard value-based reinforcement learning
procedure. The model interacts with the traffic environment to
collect state transitions, actions, rewards, and subsequent states
((𝑠,𝑎,𝑟,𝑠′)), where the stepwise reward is defined to be inversely
proportional to queue lengths at each intersection. These tran-
sitions are stored in replay memory for off-policy updates. The
optimization objective minimizes the Bellman error

This optimizer is particularly well suited to the present setting

For a single traffic prompt, multiple completions can be sampled
efficiently, parsed into candidate signal phases, and scored by the
frozen DQN critic, after which GRPO uses the relative critic rewards
within the sampled group to improve the policy. This way, critic-
guided GRPO transfers decision-making knowledge from the value-
based controller into the LLM. Although the critic is trained on
traffic data from a specific city, the LLM is not fine-tuned to overfit
any single city. Rather, it is trained to have stronger reasoning
patterns for mapping textual traffic states to better signal actions.
This strengthens the model’s traffic decision-making capacity while
preserving transferability.
4.5
End-to-End DGLight Training Procedure
Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete DGLight training loop.
In practice, the rollout collection and GRPO optimization stages are
decoupled. A full rollout episode is first collected with the frozen
critic, and the resulting prompt-score records are then used as a
separate training set for the subsequent GRPO update. This sepa-
ration enables finer-grained optimization, since multiple manual
updates can be performed on the same episodic rollout data.

5
Experiments
In this section, I evaluate DGLight to address the following research
questions:
• RQ1: (Effectiveness) Can DGLight outperform traditional,
RL-based, and existing LLM-based traffic signal control
methods on standard TSC datasets?


Yu
• RQ2: (Transferability) Does DGLight retain strong per-
formance when evaluated on city datasets that were not
used to train the DQN critic?
• RQ3: (Interpretability) Are the decisions produced by
DGLight interpretable, in the sense that its generated rea-
soning reflects the traffic conditions that motivate the se-
lected phase?
• RQ4: (Ablation Study) How much improvement comes
from critic-guided GRPO, as compared with baseline and
intermediate models?

5.1.1
Dataset. Experiments are conducted on standard traffic sig-
nal control benchmarks. Table 1 shows the final dataset statistics.
5.1.2
Environment. All methods are evaluated in an environment
built on top of CityFlow (Tang et al., 2019), a scalable microscopic
traffic simulator widely used in traffic signal control research. For
each dataset, the simulator loads the corresponding road-network
and traffic-flow configuration and exposes lane-level observations
at every control step. In my experiments, each intersection con-
nects four lane sections: east, west, north, and south. The control
action space therefore contains four signal phases: ETWT (through
movements from east and west), ELWL (left turns from east and
west), NTST (through movements from north and south), and NLSL
(left turns from north and south). Right-turn movements are always
allowed in the simulation. Each controller selects one signal phase
for every controlled intersection, after which the environment ad-
vances under a shared signal-switching interval. The green phase
duration is fixed at 30 seconds. Each green phase is followed by a
3-second yellow phase and a 2-second all-red interval to ensure safe
signal transitions. Unless otherwise stated, all compared methods
use the same simulator configuration, decision interval, and evalu-
ation protocol so that performance differences can be attributed to
the controller rather than the environment setup.
5.1.3
Baselines. The comparison includes traditional controllers,
RL-based methods, and LLM-based methods.

Results on TSC Datasets (RQ1)
Table 5 shows that DGLight is the strongest overall method among
the four LLM-based controllers. It achieves the best performance on
most datasets and metrics, with Hangzhou-1 as the main exception.
Overall, this result shows that the proposed method is superior
to the reward-discounting baselines and that critic-guided GRPO
improves the quality of the traffic-signal decisions produced by the
LLM policy.
When compared with the strongest RL baselines in Table 4, DGLight
remains competitive with the CoLight family and even exceeds
them on some metrics, showing that the proposed training proce-
dure improves the model’s reasoning ability for traffic situations.
The main exception is Hangzhou-1, where the CoLight family per-
forms exceptionally well because those models are trained directly
on that dataset, which may partly reflect overfitting to that setting.
Finally, JS-GRPO-h6 generally performs better than JS-GRPO-h3,
suggesting that a longer horizon for discounted cumulative reward
provides a better estimate of the true long-term reward.
5.3
Transferability to Unseen Cities (RQ2)
The transferability results show that DGLight retains strong perfor-
mance on datasets that were not used to fit the DQN critic, namely
all three Jinan datasets and Hangzhou-2. More importantly, the mag-
nitude of improvement is relatively larger on these unseen datasets
than on the datasets most closely aligned with the critic, especially
when compared with both the RL baselines and LightGPT. This
pattern suggests that the proposed method does not merely adapt
to the critic’s judgment, but instead improves the model’s ability
to reason about traffic states in a way that generalizes beyond the
data seen by the critic.

5.5
Ablation Study (RQ4)
This ablation isolates two sources of improvement: traffic-specific
LLM adaptation and critic-guided reinforcement learning. The un-
tuned Llama3-8b measures the capability of the base model with-
out TSC adaptation, LightGPT measures the gain from prior TSC-
specific training, and DGLight measures the additional benefit of
the proposed critic-guided GRPO procedure.
Here, DGLight-iter0 denotes the model after one round of rollout
collection followed by one round of GRPO optimization, while
DGLight-iter1 denotes the model after two such rounds. The abla-
tion shows a clear overall trend: moving from the untuned Llama3-
8b model to LightGPT yields the largest improvement, confirming
the value of traffic-specific adaptation, and critic-guided GRPO then
provides additional gains beyond the inherited LightGPT check-
point. The comparison between DGLight-iter0 and DGLight-iter1
suggests that the first round already captures most of the improve-
ment, while the second round produces smaller and more mixed
changes that mainly refine an already strong policy.
6
Discussion
In the interim report, I proposed using Group-in-Group Policy Op-
timization (GiGPO) for the TSC task, by grouping together near-
identical traffic intersection states before computing group-relative
advantages. Specifically, the idea was to define a tolerance thresh-
old on lane vehicle counts and treat two states as belonging to the
same group when the vehicle numbers on every incoming lane
differed by no more than that threshold. The motivation was that
larger groups of comparable states might improve the stability of
advantage estimation during optimization.
In the final system, however, this idea was not carried out. The first
reason is practical: in the benchmark traffic datasets used in this
study, the number of vehicles on each lane is usually small, often
fewer than ten. Under this scale, it is difficult to choose a tolerance
threshold that is both meaningful and robust.
The second reason is methodological and is ultimately more im-
portant. The implemented rollout collection method does not store
trajectory-specific cumulative rewards in the way GiGPO is de-
signed to exploit. Instead, for each observed traffic state, the pipeline
records the critic-estimated action values for all admissible signal
phases. During the GRPO optimization step, groups can therefore
be generated directly by sampling multiple completions for the
same prompt and comparing the actions they propose under the
stored action-value vector. In other words, the GRPO groups in the
final design can be chosen largely according to compute-capacity
considerations during optimization rather than by retroactively
matching similar states across trajectories.
In summary, GiGPO enlarges GRPO comparison groups so that
the resulting advantage estimates are more informative, especially

7
Conclusion and Future Work
7.1
Summary of Contributions
This dissertation presented DGLight, a critic-guided reinforcement-
learning framework for adapting a large language model to traffic
signal control. The study combined a reimplemented CoLight-based
DQN critic with a GRPO-based policy optimization procedure so
that a pretrained LLM could be trained using dense traffic-aware
action values rather than only short-horizon environment rewards.
The resulting pipeline converts structured intersection states into
textual prompts, generates interpretable reasoning traces together
with signal decisions, and reuses stored per-action value vectors to
support efficient offline policy optimization.
Empirically, the study showed that DGLight is the strongest overall
method among the compared LLM-based controllers on the se-
lected CityFlow benchmarks, while remaining competitive with
strong RL baselines. The results also suggest that critic-guided
GRPO improves transferability beyond the city used to fit the critic
and preserves the interpretability benefit of language-based traf-
fic control. Taken together, these findings show that value-based
traffic knowledge can be transferred into an LLM policy without
discarding human-readable reasoning.
7.2
Future Work
7.2.1
Token-Level Reward Assignment. The current training pipeline
assigns a reward at the completion level, which means that all gen-
erated tokens are optimized under the same response-level signal.
In practice, however, some tokens mainly serve formatting pur-
poses, such as section headers, boilerplate phrases, or the fixed
decision tag format. These tokens should not necessarily receive
the same credit assignment as the tokens that express traffic anal-
ysis or the final signal choice. A promising extension is therefore
to introduce token-level reward assignment or token masking, so
that structurally required formatting tokens are excluded from op-
timization or given reduced weight, while informative reasoning
tokens and action-selection tokens receive stronger supervision.
This may improve training efficiency by aligning the optimization
signal more closely with the parts of the output that actually matter
for decision quality.
7.2.2
MLLM-Style Training with a Traffic Situation Encoder. An-
other promising direction is to move beyond purely text-serialized
traffic states and train an MLLM-style architecture with a dedicated
traffic situation encoder. Instead of describing lane counts, queue
lengths, and neighboring conditions only through hand-crafted
text, a learned encoder could first transform the structured traffic
state into a dense embedding that captures the spatial and numer-
ical relationships in the intersection. The language model could
then condition on this embedding to generate the same text-based
reasoning and final signal decision as in the current framework.
Such a design may reduce prompt engineering overhead, shorten
the effective input length, and preserve more of the original traffic
structure, while still retaining the key advantage of interpretable
natural-language outputs.

training as the critic score vector q𝑖,𝑡in the main method, but it is
obtained indirectly through joint rollout evaluation.
Collect-then-train split. In implementation, the variant is organized
as a collect-then-train pipeline. A rollout stage first saves prompt
records, selected actions, and projected action-score vectors ob-
tained from snapshot-forked candidate evaluation. The GRPO stage
then reloads these records and fine-tunes the LLM policy using
the same prompt-conditioned reward lookup mechanism as in the
main method.

Abstract: Traffic signal control (TSC) plays a central role in reducing con- gestion and maintaining urban mobility. This dissertation intro- duces DGLight, a critic-guided reinforcement-learning framework for adapting a pretrained large language model to TSC. DGLight first trains a CoLight-based Deep Q-Network critic to estimate traffic-aware action values from structured intersection states, then uses the frozen critic to score candidate language-model actions and optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The resulting controller maps traffic states to interpretable reasoning traces and signal decisions while learning from dense per-state supervision rather than raw cumulative environment rewards. Experiments on TSC benchmarks covering Jinan and Hangzhou show that DGLight is the strongest overall method among the compared LLM-based controllers, remains competi- tive with strong RL baselines, and transfers well to city datasets not used to fit the critic. Qualitative examples further show that the model’s generated reasoning is interpretable and aligned with the chosen signal phase. The project code is available at https: //github.com/yyccbb/FYP_LLMTSC.
